title: Sequential Bayesian Updating across Two Positive Tests
description: Compute P(+) and P(D | +) from prior = 0.01, sens = 0.90, and fpr = 0.05 using Bayes' rule, then use that posterior as prior2 for a second positive test.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Set the initial disease prevalence `prior = 0.01` ($P(D)$), test sensitivity `sens = 0.90` ($P(+ \mid D)$), and false-positive rate `fpr = 0.05` ($P(+ \mid \lnot D)$).
Compute total probability `evidence = sens * prior + fpr * (1 - prior)` ($P(+)$). Apply Bayes' rule `posterior = sens * prior / evidence` ($P(D \mid +)$), then print both to 4 decimal places.
For a second independent positive test, set `prior2 = posterior`. Recompute `evidence2 = sens * prior2 + fpr * (1 - prior2)`. Print the updated posterior `sens * prior2 / evidence2` ($P(D \mid ++)$).
Look at line 11 (`prior2 = posterior`): sequential Bayesian updating takes the posterior from the first observation (`0.1538`) and uses it as the prior entering the second observation.

steps.question: Why does `P(D | ++)` on line 13 jump to `0.7660` when the first positive test only reached `P(D | +) = 0.1538`?
steps.answer: The second test starts from `prior2 = 0.1538` instead of `0.01`. Thus, `sens * prior2` (`0.90 * 0.1538`) is now much larger than the false-positive term `fpr * (1 - prior2)`.

steps.description: After the first positive test, `posterior` is `sens * prior / evidence`, printing `P(D | +)  = 0.1538`.
Using the first posterior as `prior2` for the second positive test prints `P(D | ++) = 0.7660`.
